title: New Developments in Diagrammatic Monte Carlo for Interacting Lattice Fermions: Efficient Algorithms and Applications
abstract: This thesis develops diagrammatic methods for thermodynamic and subsystem quantities of interacting lattice fermions, providing reference calculations for quantum simulators and many-body approximations. I formulate an inverse-flavour expansion about a self-consistent Hartree saddle, enumerate non-Gaussian diagrams, and use a discrete Lehmann representation to integrate selected internal vertices analytically. Density results cover 31 state points of the six-flavour Hubbard model on a $70\times70$ lattice at $T/t=0.15$.   I generalize combinatorial summation to flavour-dependent propagators and expansion shifts. CoS++ combines partial contractions to obtain connected sums for interaction subsets. A determinant-polynomial sieve evaluates the same sums through local coefficient filters; at ninth order it is 24--25 times faster than the specified CoS baselines in three-flavour dense-random-matrix benchmarks. Thermodynamic applications include a 2048-site honeycomb lattice and a three-flavour square lattice with 1024 sites.   For the second Renyi entropy, I derive a fermionic replica path integral and a stable evaluation of its two-time Green functions. The connected-determinant calculation reaches tenth order on a $3\times3$ cluster and ninth order on larger lattices. On $50\times50$ sites at $(U/t,μ/t,βt)=(3,1,8)$, the ninth-order continuation at shift $α=1.3$ gives $S_2/N_s=0.06695$ with propagated Monte Carlo uncertainty $3.0\times10^{-5}$. Comparing two expansion shifts at their respective retained orders gives an endpoint difference of $2.6\times10^{-4}$.
summary: This work presents advanced diagrammatic Monte Carlo methods for calculating thermodynamic and entanglement properties of interacting lattice fermions, particularly using the Hubbard model. The authors introduce highly efficient algorithms, such as a determinant-polynomial sieve, to manage complex diagrammatic summations. The results provide quantitative benchmarks for quantities like density and Rényi entropy, offering crucial theoretical tools for simulating quantum materials.
main_problem: The paper addresses the calculation of thermodynamic and subsystem quantities for interacting lattice fermions, aiming to provide precise theoretical benchmarks for quantum simulators.
main_result: The authors developed highly efficient diagrammatic methods, achieving significant speedups (24-25 times faster) in connected sum calculations and providing quantitative results for the second Rényi entropy on large lattices.
method: The core methodology involves developing diagrammatic Monte Carlo techniques, utilizing an inverse-flavour expansion around a Hartree saddle point, and employing advanced summation techniques like the determinant-polynomial sieve.
model_or_system: The primary model is the interacting lattice fermion system, specifically exemplified by the six-flavour Hubbard model on lattices like $70	imes70$ and honeycomb lattices. The Hamiltonian involves hopping ($t$), onsite interaction ($U$), and chemical potential ($\mu$).
key_observables: Density, double occupancy, and the second Rényi entropy ($S_2/N_s$) are key observables. Subsystem purity is also calculated using the replica path integral.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the ratio of interaction to hopping ($U/t$), chemical potential ($\mu/t$), and inverse temperature ($ eta t$). Calculations are performed across multiple state points and lattice sizes.
main_assumptions: The work relies on developing expansions (inverse-flavour expansion) and making approximations regarding the summation of diagrams, though convergence checks are performed by comparing different expansion shifts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate various diagram topologies, density estimates, benchmarks comparing the efficiency of the new summation sieve against older CoS baselines, and results for entropy calculations.
paper_structure: The paper builds from developing the foundational diagrammatic methods (inverse-flavour expansion, CoS++) to applying these methods to calculate specific thermodynamic quantities (density) and complex subsystem measures (Rényi entropy) using replica path integrals.
why_interesting: The rigorous development of diagrammatic techniques and the focus on calculating entanglement measures like Rényi entropy in lattice fermion models are highly relevant to understanding quantum correlations in strongly correlated systems, which is a major theme in AMO physics.

Figure 2.2: Cumulative density estimates in Table 2.2, ﬁrst reported in Ref. [1], for the 70 × 70 square-lattice SU(6) Hubbard model at T/t = 0.15. The curves show the saddle result, the saddle plus the RPA correction, and the sum through O(1/Nf). Error bars give the ﬁnal-sum uncertainties listed in the table; the saddle and saddle-plus-RPA curves are deterministic numerical values. Lines are guides to the eye. Vertical separations give the density change produced by each correction.

Figure 2.3: Additive density contributions at the state points of Fig. 2.2. The RPA increment is deterministic. The ﬁrst non-Gaussian increment is δn1/Nf = n≤1/Nf −nsp −δnRPA, with the same absolute Monte Carlo uncertainty as the cumulative density. All panels share the same vertical scale, and lines are guides to the eye. The non-Gaussian contribution varies with ﬁlling as well as interaction strength.
